title: Dynamics and Mechanisms of Sudden Free Drainage in Saturated Media
content:
Abstract

Sudden free drainage in saturated media under gravity is widespread and potentially destructive, yet its controlling mechanisms remain poorly understood. To address this knowledge gap, this study conducted 77 one-dimensional sudden free drainage experiments covering particle sizes of 2.0–20.0 mm, porosities of 0.40–1, water temperatures of 22.2°C–95.4°C, and salinity of 0–40 g/L. The rapid evolution of the water level was captured using high-speed videography with high spatial and temporal resolution. Results indicate that structural factors of the filling medium (directional packing density, particle size, and porosity) dominate drainage dynamics, followed by water temperature, whereas salinity has a minor effect under the tested inert glass-bead conditions. Based on experimental observations and mechanistic analysis, we developed a physically motivated, lumped semi-empirical model, named the Modified Free-Fall Water Level Model (MFFM), to describe the water-level evolution during sudden, gravity-driven, one-dimensional drainage. The model fits closely match experimental data (mostly R 2 > 0.99, RMSE < 5 cm), demonstrating the model's good performance within the tested configurations. Moreover, a strong log–log linear correlation (R 2 = 0.98) is observed between the MFFM parameter and a structural index of the uniform medium, defined by particle size, porosity, and directional packing density, indicating a robust physical underpinning. The results demonstrate that rapid drainage evolves through a transient balance between gravitational driving and medium-induced resistance. This study provides a laboratory-scale framework for understanding the inertia-dominated and non-Darcy drainage processes that may be relevant to rapid drainage through highly permeable geological pathways.
